tags.gist: Welcomes the discussion paper and the chance to help shape a proportionate approach to GenAI-enabled devices.
Recommends the unit of assessment be the complete sociotechnical system, from source evidence and controls to human authority and lifecycle monitoring, not the model alone.
Wants the activity-and-consequence framework to account explicitly for evidence traceability, independent reviewability, reversibility and time to harm.
Wants omission, contradiction, under-escalation and over-escalation measured separately rather than folded into one accuracy score.
Would add evidence fidelity and provenance to premarket competency, with clinical confirmation done in the intended deployed configuration.
Wants evaluation to measure human-AI team performance, including automation bias, usability, comprehension and escalation pathway effectiveness.
Wants monitoring and change control triggered by material changes anywhere in the system, including model versions, prompts, retrieval, tools and population.
Says voluntary master files could give downstream developers more transparency while keeping confidential information protected.
Would regulate agentic systems by the authority they exercise, reversibility of actions, safeguards and the chance for timely human intervention.
Argues safety depends on the whole clinical system's architecture, with evidence, controls, reasoning, verification, escalation, human authority and monitoring kept separate.
Supports the competency-based lifecycle direction with four additions: a provenance competency, separate escalation metrics, tested oversight and authority-based agentic rules.
Lists eight recommendations, from a layered safety architecture and a provenance competency to event-triggered revalidation, master files and authority-based agentic controls.
Describes how GenAI differs from deterministic software: open inputs, variable outputs, tool use and behavior that shifts as models and prompts evolve.
Notes the paper's direction matches FDA lifecycle and PCCP guidance, IMDRF machine learning principles, WHO guidance and the NIST GenAI profile.
Would make the complete socio-technical system, including oversight and monitoring, the object of regulatory and safety analysis rather than one model.
Describes four architecture layers: provenance-preserving source evidence, deterministic safety controls, bounded generative reasoning and verification of outputs against evidence.
Would design escalation as a safety function, giving serious under-escalation substantially more weight than low-consequence over-escalation.
Wants human oversight to be operational, with reviewers given the information, time and interface needed to question or overrule the system.
Treats monitoring and revalidation as part of the safety architecture, since deployed systems change, and notes FDA's lifecycle work already moves this way.
Backs the two-axis concept as a foundation and proposes four modifiers: evidence traceability, independent reviewability, reversibility and time to harm.
Would not rate patient-facing systems high risk merely for lacking a clinician user; proposes functional categories from organisation to action direction.
Wants critical and non-critical under- and over-escalation reported separately, with red-flag sensitivity evaluated apart from overall accuracy.
Supports the competency-based direction and agrees competency must attach to the configured deployed system, since a model benchmark alone proves nothing.
Proposes an added competency, evidence fidelity and provenance, covering faithful patient data, source context, separating inference from fact and flagging gaps.
Accepts the human-AI configuration as evaluation unit where supervision is intended, but says a human in the loop proves nothing unless oversight is real.
Finds more premarket uncertainty potentially acceptable for lower-risk functions with reversible outputs, effective review, rapid rollback, full logging and limited autonomy.
Suggests a progressive deployment path from shadow mode to monitored use, with no presumed flexibility for irreversible or life-critical functions.
Wants periodic review plus event-triggered reassessment, monitoring hallucination, omissions, escalation errors, drift, component changes, overrides and automation bias.
Lists reassessment triggers such as model updates, prompt or tool changes, new populations and new failure modes, within a validate-observe-correct-revalidate loop.
Supports the master file principle because downstream developers hold responsibility while lacking full information about the model they depend on.
Lists master file contents from version identifiers and failure modes to update cadence and deprecation, and says the file is no approval of the model.
Recommends regulating agentic systems partly by their authority to act, under a graduated authority model, not only a technical definition of agent.
Wants audit records of plans, tools, approvals and actions at higher authority levels, with mandatory human checkpoints for irreversible actions unless evidence justifies otherwise.
Wants source evidence kept distinguishable from generated interpretation throughout the lifecycle, with interfaces separating report, result, rule, inference and decision.
Says deterministic logic should handle safety-critical checks it suits while generative reasoning handles contextual tasks, so no single probabilistic component is the only protection.
Says provider updates can change behavior without any code change, so a clinically relevant behavioral change should trigger evaluation on its own.
Recommends a controlled model registry and a detection, quarantine, evaluation, approval and controlled deployment path for material model changes.
Lists the validation domains, from evidence fidelity and omission to model change and human-AI team, the commenter would use instead of one accuracy metric.
Wants named responsibility for model approval, monitoring, incident review and rollback, with change control triggered by model, tool, prompt, population or drift events.
Finds the paper notable for treating GenAI oversight as a problem of systems, since model-level benchmark accuracy alone misses important risks.
Explains how the layered architecture makes risks governable by separating provenance, deterministic controls, reasoning, verification, escalation, human authority and monitoring.
Acknowledges limits: layering alone does not prove safety, rules can be wrong, and clinicians can still over-rely, so empirical validation remains needed.
Says the activity and consequence approach, enhanced with traceability, reversibility, reviewability and time to harm, offers a plausible route to proportionate control.
Says the regulatory objective should be to make GenAI's probabilistic risks observable, measurable, bounded and accountable rather than to eliminate them.
Recommends a seven-layer framework with a provenance competency, severity-weighted metrics, tested oversight, change-triggered revalidation and authority-based agentic requirements.
